Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Miller, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these early weeks of motherhood. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS. It’s a well-studied 10-question tool that helps us see how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you might harm yourself or someone else, and then we’ll talk together about immediate safety. We’ll go question by question; just answer in your own words—no right or wrong responses. Ready to start?

Question 1: Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my partner makes a silly face at the baby—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. I catch myself having to “try” to find things funny instead of just naturally laughing along.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I can still laugh, but it feels like I have to remind myself to do it—like it doesn’t just bubble up the way it used to before the baby.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my morning coffee—but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It’s more like “that’ll be nice” instead of really counting down the minutes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like if the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I catch myself thinking maybe I’m just not doing something obvious. It’s not constant, but it pops up a couple of times this week—this little voice saying I “should” know better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Every now and then I’ll suddenly feel a wave of worry—like, is he breathing okay in the crib, or am I missing something the doctor warned us about? It usually passes once I check on him, but it hits without any real warning.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicked—more like a quick flutter of “what-if” that shows up and then leaves once I peek at him or take a breath. It doesn’t stick around long enough to feel like a real scare, just a brief jolt.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When the laundry’s piled up and he won’t nap, I feel like I’m juggling more than I can hold—but I usually manage to get through the list once he finally settles. It’s stressful in the moment, though.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, nothing that strong. I might lie awake for a little while if I’m replaying the day, but once I’m actually trying to sleep, I drift off okay. It’s more trouble getting my mind to quiet down, not real unhappiness keeping me up.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’ve had moments—maybe once or twice this week—where I just felt kind of heavy and teary, usually when I’m alone with the baby in the late afternoon. It passes after a little cry or if my partner comes home and distracts me, but it’s definitely there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times—like yesterday when he wouldn’t latch and I felt stuck on the couch—but it’s not all day or anything. The tears come, I wipe them away, and I keep going; it’s not this constant waterfall.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get worn out, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 11: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary – 06 Jun 2024

Symptoms endorsed
- Anhedonia: reduced spontaneous laughter and anticipatory enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Low mood: intermittent “heavy, teary” spells, usually late afternoon (Q8)  
- Crying spells: 2 episodes this week (Q9)  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame: “should know better” when baby fussy (Q3)  
- Anxiety: sudden, unprovoked “what-if” worries about infant safety; quick physical jolt but resolves rapidly (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed: “juggling more than I can hold,” especially during infant nap refusal (Q6)  
- Sleep: difficulty quieting thoughts at bedtime, but able to fall asleep without persistent mood-related insomnia (Q7)

Frequency / Severity indicators
- Mood symptoms mild-to-moderate, intermittent (not daily)  
- No impairment in basic self-care or infant care  
- No current suicidal ideation, intent, or plan (Q10)

Risk factors
- First-time parenting stress  
- Limited spontaneous support during late-afternoon/evening hours (partner returns home only then)  
- Absence of personal or family psychiatric history noted but not explored

Safety
- Denies self-harm thoughts; no protective concerns voiced

Screening impression
- Subsyndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms present; do not meet full criteria for major depression but suggestive of adjustment difficulties with mixed depressive-anxiety features in the postpartum period.

Recommend (routine)
- Continue monitoring with Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at next pediatric or postpartum visit; consider structured follow-up within 2 weeks to reassess symptom trajectory and coping.
